We've known for years that weight gain or loss comes down to basic physics: conservation of energy

Food energy intake = food energy used + food energy stored + food energy expelled

Substituting the terms:

Calories consumed = calories used + calories stored (generally, as fat) + calories excreted in waste

That's all there is to it. You want to minimise your calories stored as fat? Do any combination of the following while holding the others equal:

  • Consume less energy in your food: eat less foods and/or eat foods of lower energy density. Fat is the highest energy-density food, so any increases in your fat intake (as a proportion of total mass of food consumed) need to be offset by decreases in the amount you eat, or by other adjustments below. (source: it's all over the internet - I'm sure you can find a source)

  • Decrease energy stored by increasing the amount of energy your body uses: e.g. through exercise. I'm told that increasing muscle mass increases the amount of energy your body uses in simply keeping you alive - so, build muscle mass (while holding the other factors equal) if you need to lose weight. (source: my high school education and the sports science degree that my personal trainer completed)

  • Manipulate your diet so that your body can use or store less of the energy contained in the food you eat. You could try to substitute complex carbohydrates in the place of simple ones, or substitute protein in the place of carbohydrates, etc. But each person's body reacts a little differently, and some are able to better adapt to different energy sources than others. Evidently, this is the most complex of the options, and I would not recommend you attempt to lose weight using this option.
